hero.title: Entrepreneurship: test ideas before you bet on them
hero.subtitle: Write problem statements, canvases and pitches in a document editor, and work out break-even, cash and customer economics in a working spreadsheet. Every task is checked and explained.
hero.outcomeLine: After this course you can validate an idea, model its numbers and pitch it clearly.

assessment: Finish the required labs in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (70% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Complete the business plan and the final assessment.

faq.q: Do I need a business idea to start?
faq.a: No. The first module shows how to find problems worth solving. You can use an idea you already have or the examples in the course.

faq.q: Will this teach me company registration and tax?
faq.a: It gives a checklist of what to find out. Rules differ by country, so you should consult a qualified adviser for legal and tax matters.

faq.q: Can I get investors with this?
faq.a: No course can promise funding. It teaches how to test ideas, model the numbers and pitch clearly.

activities.title: Write a problem statement
activities.objective: Describe who has the problem, what it is, how big it is and how they cope today.
activities.scenario: You noticed that students in your college struggle to find affordable, healthy lunch. Write the problem statement.
steps: Add a Heading 2 'Who'.
Add Heading 2 sections: Problem, Size, Today.
In Who describe the customer in one sentence.
In Size include a number (for example how many students and how much they spend).
In Today describe how they cope now and why that is not good enough.
Keep it between 90 and 220 words.

checks.label: Four sections
checks.hint: Use Heading 2 for Who, Problem, Size and Today.
checks.explain: A clear structure keeps the statement honest.

checks.label: A number in Size
checks.hint: Include a number such as 3000 students.
checks.explain: Numbers show whether the problem is big enough.

checks.label: A cost is shown
checks.explain: A problem matters when it costs something.

spec.what: a cost in rupees or time

checks.label: Current alternatives
checks.explain: Competition is whatever customers do now.

activities.title: Write customer interview questions
activities.objective: Ask about past behaviour, not opinions about your idea.
activities.scenario: You want to learn whether students would use a lunch subscription. Write eight interview questions that avoid leading questions.
steps: Write a numbered list of at least six questions.
Start with questions about what they did last time, such as 'Tell me about the last time you ...'.
Ask about cost and frequency.
Ask what they use now and what they dislike about it.
Do not ask 'Would you use my app?'.

checks.label: A numbered list of six or more questions
checks.explain: A set of questions is easier to run.

checks.label: Questions about past behaviour
checks.explain: Past behaviour predicts more than opinions.

spec.re: last time|tell me about|walk me through
spec.what: a question about the last time

checks.label: Questions about cost or frequency
checks.hint: Ask how often or how much.

spec.what: a question about how often or how much
a question about what they use today

checks.label: Avoids the leading question
checks.hint: Do not write 'Would you use' or 'Do you like my'.
checks.explain: Leading questions give polite, useless answers.

spec.re: ^(?!.*(would you use|do you like my|would you buy)).*$

checks.label: Between 60 and 200 words
checks.explain: Short questions are easier to ask.

activities.title: Unit economics and break-even
activities.objective: Work out profit per unit, break-even volume and profit at a target volume.
activities.scenario: The lunch business sells meals at 100 rupees. Each meal costs 60 rupees in ingredients and packaging. Fixed monthly costs (cook, helper, space) are 36,000 rupees.
steps: In B6 work out the profit per meal (the contribution): price minus variable cost.
In B7 work out the contribution margin as a share of the price.
In B8 find the break-even number of meals per month: fixed costs divided by contribution, rounded up with ROUNDUP.
In B9 work out the profit at the target volume: contribution times meals minus fixed costs.
In B10 show Viable if the profit is positive, else Not yet.

checks.label: B6 is the profit per meal
B8 is the break-even volume
checks.explain: Fixed costs divided by contribution; round up.

checks.label: B9 is the profit at target
checks.explain: Contribution times meals minus fixed costs.

checks.label: B10 is the verdict
checks.explain: Positive profit at the target means viable.

activities.title: Plan the first six months
activities.objective: Forecast revenue and costs month by month, find the cash position and the lowest point.
activities.scenario: A start-up begins with 50,000 rupees. Revenue grows each month and costs are mostly fixed. Work out profit and cash for six months.
steps: In D2 enter the profit: revenue minus costs. Fill down to D7.
In E2 enter the cash at the end of month 1: starting cash in B9 plus D2.
In E3 enter =E2+D3 and fill down to E7.
In B10 find the lowest cash balance with MIN.
In B11 show Safe if the lowest cash is above zero, otherwise Raise money.

checks.label: D2 is the profit in month 1
E2 is the cash after month 1
E4 is the cash after month 3
E7 is the cash after month 6
B11 is the verdict
checks.explain: If cash falls below zero you need funding.

activities.title: Customer acquisition cost versus lifetime value
activities.objective: Check that a customer is worth more than they cost to win.
activities.scenario: The lunch business spends on posters and offers to win subscribers. Each subscriber pays 450 rupees a week with a 40% margin and stays 8 weeks on average.
steps: In B7 work out the customer acquisition cost (CAC): marketing spend divided by new customers.
In B8 work out the lifetime value (LTV): weekly price times margin times weeks stayed.
In B9 work out the LTV to CAC ratio.
In B10 show Healthy if the ratio is at least 3, otherwise Improve.
In B11 work out the payback in weeks: CAC divided by weekly profit per customer (price times margin).

checks.label: B7 is CAC
checks.explain: What each customer cost to win.

checks.label: B10 is the verdict
checks.explain: A ratio of 3 or more is a common healthy sign.

activities.title: Write a one-minute pitch
activities.objective: Pitch the business clearly: problem, solution, traction, ask.
activities.scenario: Write a pitch of about 150 words for the lunch business, to be spoken in one minute to a panel of judges.
steps: Start with the problem and a number.
Describe the solution in one sentence.
Give one piece of traction (customers, pilot results or a signed agreement).
State the business model and price.
End with a clear ask, such as an amount and how you would spend it.
Keep it between 100 and 220 words.

checks.label: Gives traction
checks.hint: Mention customers, a pilot or sales.

spec.what: traction such as a pilot or customers

checks.label: States the price
checks.explain: A business must say how it earns.

checks.label: Ends with an ask
checks.explain: A pitch ends with a request.

activities.title: Final project: a one-page business plan
activities.objective: Bring the problem, customer, model, numbers and next steps together on one page.
activities.scenario: Write a one-page business plan for a small venture you could start in your area: a service, product or app.
steps: Add a Heading 1 with the business name.
Add Heading 2 sections: Problem and customer, Solution, Business model, Numbers, Risks, Next 90 days.
Under Numbers include the price, the cost per unit and the break-even volume.
Under Next 90 days write a numbered list of at least four actions with dates or weeks.
Under Risks list at least two risks with a response each.
Keep it between 180 and 380 words.

checks.label: Six sections
checks.explain: A plan covers all the essentials.

checks.label: Sections in order
checks.hint: Problem and customer, Solution, Business model, Numbers, Risks, Next 90 days.
checks.explain: From why to how to what next.

checks.label: A price and break-even
checks.hint: Write a price and a break-even number.
checks.explain: Numbers test whether the idea can work.
